title: Approximate Graph Propagation Revisited: Dynamic Parameterized Queries, Tighter Bounds and Dynamic Updates

problem.claim: Approximate Graph Propagation must support evolving graphs and query parameters specified dynamically for application needs.

gap.claim: Existing AGP-Static approaches rely on an unavailable optimal subset-sampling algorithm and perform poorly on dynamic graphs, requiring extra O(log2 n) query overhead and O(n log n) time per update.

contributions.claim: AGP-Static can be adapted to support dynamic parameterized queries.
AGP-Static++ is a simpler algorithm that reduces query complexity by roughly O(log2 n) while preserving AGP-Static's approximation guarantees.
AGP-Dynamic achieves O(1) amortized time per graph update while preserving the query complexity and approximation guarantees.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly distinguish AGP-Static++ and AGP-Dynamic as proposed algorithms addressing unresolved query and dynamic-update challenges.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Comprehensive experiments reportedly show speedups of up to 177× for updates and 10× for queries compared with baselines.

narrative_sequence.summary: AGP is presented as a unified framework covering several graph propagation tasks.
The work targets dynamic graphs and dynamically specified query parameters.
AGP-Static has unresolved query-sampling assumptions and poor dynamic-graph update performance.
AGP-Static++ improves query complexity, while AGP-Dynamic improves amortized update time.
Experiments report substantial update and query speedups over baselines.

source_observation.claim: Separating query processing from graph-update maintenance is associated with distinct complexity improvements in the proposed algorithms.

interpretation.claim: Dynamic graph systems may benefit from independently optimizing query-time and update-time paths.

application.claim: When designing evolving graph propagation systems, evaluate query latency and update cost as separate performance objectives.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether these bounds or benefits hold for workloads beyond the reported setting.

unknowns: The algorithms' implementation details and exact query-complexity formulas are not provided.
The experimental datasets, baselines, workload configuration, and statistical methodology are unspecified.
The approximation guarantees are not quantified.
The abstract does not identify the conditions under which the reported speedups were obtained.
